goldBar.Name: Gold
goldBar.Description: Gold bars traded through Dejima, the next main export following silver.

goldBar2.Name: Gold
goldBar2.Description: To ensure enough domestic supply gold became a banned export in 1763.

copperCoin.Name: Copper Coin
copperCoin.Description: Standard domestic currency. Export of ordinary copper coinage was strictly forbidden.

cross.Name: Christian Cross
cross.Description: A symbol of the banned Christian faith, strictly prohibited under the Sakoku edicts, but highly desired by the hidden Christians.

rawSilk.Name: Raw Silk
rawSilk.Description: Unprocessed silk bundled for export, a staple of early Dejima trade.

silkRoll.Name: Silk Roll
silkRoll.Description: Three rolls of finished, dyed silk. Extremely expensive and highly prized by nobility, with colors that commoners cannot wear.

silver.Name: Silver
silver.Description: A silver bar, the primary export at Dejima.

silver2.Name: Silver
silver2.Description: It turns out that Japan has been producing up to a third of the silver in the world, but we have exported so much that an export ban has been put in place to ensure domestic supply.

copperBar_s.Name: Copper Bar (Small)
copperBar_s.Description: A small refined copper bar, a legal and common export from Japan throughout the Edo period.

copperBar_m.Name: Copper Bar (Medium)
copperBar_m.Description: A medium refined copper bar, a legal and common export from Japan throughout the Edo period.

copperBar_l.Name: Copper Bar (Large)
copperBar_l.Description: A large refined copper bar, a legal and common export from Japan throughout the Edo period.

nagasakiTradeCoin.Name: Nagasaki Trade Coin
nagasakiTradeCoin.Description: A specially minted copper coin authorized for foreign trade at Dejima. Made by copying other nations coins for simplicity, their production started in 1659.

nagasakiTradeCoin2.Name: Nagasaki Trade Coin
nagasakiTradeCoin2.Description: A specially minted copper coin authorized for foreign trade at Dejima. Production only ran from 1659 to 1685, but many were made.

silverware.Name: Silverware
silverware.Description: Silver tableware has become a booming export, and it isn't a silver bar so it is not under the effect of the 1668 silver export ban.

silverware2.Name: Silverware
silverware2.Description: It took some time but a new law has been passed making sure silverware is also illegal to export, it was simply being used to bypass the silver export ban.

goodsSack.Name: Goods Sack
goodsSack.Description: A large burlap sack of pepper or sugar, identified by the color of the filling. A staple of legal Dejima commerce.

camphorWood.Name: Camphor Wood
camphorWood.Description: Planks and blocks of aromatic camphor wood, valued in craftsmanship and medicine.

ceramicBowl.Name: Ceramic Bowl
ceramicBowl.Description: Fine ceramic bowls, a prized export of Japanese craftsmanship sought by Dutch traders to resell in Europe.

lacquerwareBowl.Name: Lacquerware Bowl
lacquerwareBowl.Description: Bowls finished in traditional urushi lacquer, highly sought after by Dutch traders to resell in Europe.

christianBook.Name: Christian Text
christianBook.Description: A prohibited Christian religious text, identifiable by the cross embossed on its cover.

scienceBook.Name: Scientific Text
scienceBook.Description: A European text on natural philosophy or science. Just more Western books banned alongside religious texts.

scienceBook2.Name: Scientific Text
scienceBook2.Description: A European text on natural philosophy or science. Interest in this new field called 'Dutch Studies' is slowly expanding, their religion may be dangerous but these scientific books are legal now.

opiumSmall.Name: Opium (Medical)
opiumSmall.Description: A small tray of four cloth opium balls, tolerated in limited quantities for medicinal use

opiumSmall2.Name: Opium (Medical)
opiumSmall2.Description: A small tray of four cloth opium balls, seeing the second opium war begin caused a strict ban in 1857.

opiumLarge.Name: Opium (Bulk)
opiumLarge.Description: A wooden box packed with excessive amounts of opium balls. Opium may be allowed, but only in small, very restricted amounts. This is highly illegal
